demographics: Prevalence rises steeply with age; roughly doubles every 5 years after age 65
More common in women, largely because women live longer
More common in Black and Hispanic older adults in the US, in part due to higher rates of vascular risk factors and differences in access to care
Lower educational attainment and limited cognitive reserve are associated with higher risk

risk_factors.text: Family history of dementia, especially a parent or sibling
Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
Traumatic brain injury, especially repeated injury

family_history: Dementia in a parent or sibling
Early-onset dementia in a first-degree relative (suggests a familial mutation)
Down syndrome in a family member
Parkinson disease or a movement disorder in the family
social_history: Lives alone or has limited support at home
Retired, with recent loss of structured daily routine
Drives and has had near-misses or getting lost
Family or caregiver noticing changes before the patient does
Low educational attainment or limited occupational complexity
exposures: Repeated head trauma, including contact sports or military blast exposure
Chronic use of sedating or anticholinergic medications
Occupational exposure to solvents or pesticides

chief_complaints.text: My family says I keep forgetting things
I can't remember where I put things or why I walked into a room
I got lost driving to the grocery store I've gone to for years
I'm not interested in the things I used to enjoy
I have trouble finding the right words

hpi.onset: Insidious, over months to a few years; family often dates it to a specific event such as a missed bill or a wrong turn
hpi.duration: Usually at least 6 months of progressive change by the time of presentation
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive and steady; memory and function decline over time, with the patient needing more help with finances, medications and appointments
hpi.quality: Progressive cognitive decline that interferes with everyday function; short-term memory is affected first in the most common form
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at first presentation; interferes with instrumental activities such as finances, driving and medications
hpi.timing: Constant, worse when tired or in unfamiliar settings; often more noticeable in the evening
aggravating: New medications with sedating or anticholinergic effects
relieving: Help from a spouse or adult child

associated_symptoms.text: Repeating the same question or story within minutes
Misplacing items, sometimes in odd places like the freezer
Trouble managing money, bills or medications
Word-finding difficulty and calling objects by the wrong name
Apathy and loss of interest in hobbies
Irritability or personality change noticed by family
Difficulty with orientation to date or time
Visual hallucinations, often of people or animals

pertinent_negatives: Sudden onset over hours to days
Fluctuating level of alertness or attention
New focal weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Head trauma in the days before symptoms started
Recent change in medications or new sedating drugs
Symptoms that began after starting a new drug or stopping alcohol

argues_against: Acute infection or delirium as the cause
Stroke or mass lesion as the primary cause
Gastrointestinal bleeding causing anemia and confusion

positives.text: Urinary incontinence later in the course

argues_against: Urinary tract infection causing acute confusion
Arthritis or myopathy as the cause of functional decline

atypical.how_it_differs: Very old patients may present with falls, weight loss, incontinence or delirium triggered by a minor illness rather than with memory complaints.
missing_classic_features: Clear progression described by the patient

atypical.how_it_differs: Dementia is very rare in children; when it occurs it is usually part of a metabolic, genetic or neurodegenerative disorder and presents with developmental regression, seizures or loss of previously acquired skills.

Cognitive decline may be due to an opportunistic infection of the central nervous system, such as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and can progress faster.
Uremic encephalopathy and dialysis-related fluctuations can mimic dementia; symptoms may wax and wane with dialysis and improve with treatment.
Hepatic encephalopathy causes fluctuating attention, asterixis and confusion that can look like dementia but reverses with treatment of the liver disease.
Recurrent hypoglycemia and severe hyperglycemia can cause cognitive symptoms that fluctuate with glucose levels and improve with better control.

general.mild: Well-groomed, alert, oriented to person and place but not always to date; may repeat questions; can hold a conversation with cues
general.moderate: Disheveled or dressed inappropriately for weather; oriented to person only; needs prompting to stay on topic; may be anxious or irritable
general.severe: Poorly groomed, disoriented to person, place and time; speech may be sparse or incoherent; needs help with basic activities of daily living
general.critical: Non-verbal or minimally responsive, incontinent, dependent for all care; may be mute or have swallowing difficulty

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient their name, where they are, the date and the day of the week
findings.finding: Disorientation to date and day first, then to place; orientation to person is preserved until late

findings.maneuver: Give three words, have the patient repeat them, distract for a few minutes, then ask for recall
findings.finding: Cannot recall the words even with cueing; may confabulate or repeat the same question

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to spell 'world' backward or count backward from 100 by 7s
findings.finding: Makes errors but attention is relatively preserved compared with the memory deficit; no marked fluctuation during the visit

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to draw a clock face with a specified time, or to name as many animals as possible in one minute
findings.finding: Clock is disorganized with wrong spacing or hands; verbal fluency is reduced

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to name common objects (watch, pen) and to repeat a phrase
findings.finding: Word-finding pauses, circumlocution or wrong word substitutions; repetition is relatively preserved early

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to copy a simple figure such as intersecting pentagons
findings.finding: Distorted or incomplete copy

findings.maneuver: Test pupils, extraocular movements, visual fields, facial symmetry and hearing
findings.finding: Cranial nerves are intact; no field cut, ptosis or facial droop

findings.maneuver: Test strength in the arms and legs and check for pronator drift
findings.finding: Strength is symmetric and full; no focal weakness or drift

findings.maneuver: Test deep tendon reflexes and the plantar response
findings.finding: Reflexes are symmetric and downgoing plantars; no Babinski sign

findings.maneuver: Test light touch, pinprick and vibration in the feet
findings.finding: Sensation is intact and symmetric

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to walk a few steps and turn
findings.finding: Gait is steady with a normal base; no shuffling or freezing

findings.maneuver: Observe for tremor at rest and test tone in the arms
findings.finding: No resting tremor and no cogwheel rigidity

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both arms outstretched with wrists extended
findings.finding: No flapping tremor of the hands

findings.maneuver: Check for neck stiffness and perform a brief screen for meningeal signs
findings.finding: Neck is supple; no meningeal signs
No goiter or nodule

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and check for carotid bruits
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur; no carotid bruit
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and check for hepatosplenomegaly
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic screen for focal deficits
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss, aphasia or visual field cut

labs.caveat: Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of cognitive slowing; a normal TSH makes it very unlikely.
Low B12 is a reversible cause of cognitive decline and neuropathy; check even when the CBC is normal.
Folate deficiency is uncommon in the US but is a reversible contributor when present.
Hyponatremia can cause confusion and gait instability; correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Hypercalcemia causes confusion, lethargy and constipation; consider primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy.
Both hypoglycemia and marked hyperglycemia can impair cognition; values at the extremes are more likely to be the cause of acute confusion than of chronic dementia.
Diabetes is a vascular risk factor and is associated with cognitive decline; poor control also raises the risk of hypoglycemia.
Uremia can cause encephalopathy; also guides safe dosing of cholinesterase inhibitors and other medications.
Rises with dehydration and renal impairment; a high BUN with normal creatinine can reflect poor intake.
Low albumin suggests malnutrition or chronic illness and affects corrected calcium.
Elevated transaminases raise concern for hepatic encephalopathy or alcohol-related liver disease.
Interpret with AST and the history of alcohol use.
Order only when hepatic encephalopathy is suspected; levels correlate poorly with the degree of encephalopathy.

findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm without discernible P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation
Sinus bradycardia or atrioventricular block in a patient taking a cholinesterase inhibitor or other rate-slowing drug

imaging.preferred_when: Preferred initial structural study when available

findings.text: Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci and enlarged ventricles out of proportion to age
Periventricular and deep white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (chronic microvascular disease)
Lacunar infarcts or old cortical infarcts
Normal-appearing brain for age (imaging does not exclude dementia)

imaging.preferred_when: When MRI is unavailable, contraindicated, or the patient cannot tolerate it

findings.text: Generalized cerebral atrophy with widened sulci and ventricles
White matter hypodensities from chronic small vessel disease

imaging.preferred_when: Diagnostically uncertain cases, especially early-onset or atypical presentations

findings.text: Temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism (Alzheimer pattern)
Frontal or anterior temporal hypometabolism (frontotemporal pattern)

imaging.preferred_when: Selected cases where Alzheimer disease is suspected but the diagnosis remains uncertain

findings.text: Cortical amyloid uptake indicating amyloid plaques
No cortical amyloid uptake, arguing against Alzheimer disease as the cause

imaging.preferred_when: When vascular dementia is suspected and carotid revascularization is being considered

initial.why: Screens for anemia, infection or a hematologic cause of cognitive symptoms
Detects hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, uremia and glucose abnormalities, all reversible causes of confusion
Hypothyroidism is a common and reversible cause of cognitive slowing
Deficiency is a reversible cause of cognitive decline and neuropathy
Identifies diabetes, a vascular risk factor and a cause of glucose-related cognitive fluctuation
Structural study to look for atrophy patterns, vascular disease and treatable lesions such as subdural hematoma or hydrocephalus
Alternative structural study when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated
initial.only_if: MRI cannot be obtained or the patient is unstable

confirmatory.why: Formal testing documents the pattern and severity of deficits and helps distinguish dementia from depression or normal aging

supporting.why: Reversible deficiency when the history suggests poor nutrition or alcohol use
supporting.only_if: poor nutrition, alcohol use or macrocytic anemia

supporting.why: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder can mimic dementia
supporting.only_if: risk factors or systemic features suggest HIV

supporting.why: Neurosyphilis is a treatable cause of cognitive decline

supporting.only_if: liver disease or fluctuating attention with asterixis

supporting.why: Helps distinguish dementia subtypes when the diagnosis is uncertain
supporting.only_if: early-onset or atypical presentation with an uncertain diagnosis

supporting.why: Can support or argue against Alzheimer disease when the diagnosis is uncertain
supporting.only_if: Alzheimer disease is suspected but the clinical picture is unclear

supporting.why: Assesses for carotid stenosis when vascular dementia is suspected and revascularization is being considered
supporting.only_if: vascular dementia is suspected and the patient is a candidate for revascularization

not_indicated.why: Not needed if MRI is obtained and tolerated
Not part of the routine workup; reserved for diagnostically uncertain cases
Not routine; does not change management in most patients
Not routine unless vascular dementia is suspected and revascularization is being considered
Not routine; correlates poorly with encephalopathy and is only useful when liver disease is suspected
Not routine in the absence of risk factors
Not routine in the absence of risk factors or a compatible history
Not routine for typical dementia; reserved for suspected infection, inflammation or rapidly progressive disease

decision_points: Delirium must be excluded first: acute onset, fluctuating attention and an identifiable trigger point to delirium rather than dementia
Depression can mimic dementia and should be screened for, since it is treatable
Reversible causes (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, medication effects) should be excluded before attributing decline to a neurodegenerative disease
Structural imaging is indicated once to exclude subdural hematoma, tumor, hydrocephalus and stroke
Rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months should prompt evaluation for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, autoimmune encephalitis or central nervous system infection

criteria.name: Dementia syndrome
criteria.summary: Acquired cognitive decline in one or more domains (memory, language, executive function, visuospatial ability, attention) that is severe enough to interfere with independence in daily activities and represents a decline from a prior level of function. The decline is not explained by delirium or a major psychiatric disorder, and is established by history and objective cognitive testing.
items: Cognitive decline from a previous level of performance
Impairment in at least one cognitive domain
Interference with independence in everyday activities
Not better explained by another mental disorder

differential.name: Delirium
differential.why_considered: Acute confusion in an older adult is far more often delirium than new dementia, and the two can coexist.
differential.trigger: Acute onset over hours to days with fluctuating attention

history: Onset over hours to days rather than months to years
Attention waxes and wanes through the day
Recent infection, surgery, new medication, hospitalization or withdrawal
Family reports the patient is 'not themselves' since a specific date
exam: Fluctuating level of alertness during the visit
Marked inattention on digit span or serial sevens
May be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed
Tremor, myoclonus or asterixis when metabolic or withdrawal-related
labs: BMP showing hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, uremia or glucose abnormality
Drug levels or toxicology when overdose or withdrawal is suspected
imaging: Head CT or MRI to exclude acute stroke, hemorrhage or mass when focal findings are present

differential.name: Major depressive disorder with cognitive symptoms
differential.why_considered: Depression in older adults can present with memory complaints, poor concentration and apathy that look like dementia.
differential.trigger: Prominent depressed mood, anhedonia or hopelessness alongside cognitive complaints

history: Depressed mood, tearfulness or loss of pleasure most of the day
Patient complains loudly about memory while family may not notice as much
Sleep and appetite disturbance, early morning waking
Prior episodes of depression or recent bereavement
Symptoms began after a life stressor or loss
exam: Psychomotor retardation or agitation
Poor effort on cognitive testing with 'I don't know' answers
Cognitive scores improve with encouragement and cueing
Flat affect and hopelessness
labs: TSH to exclude hypothyroidism, which can cause both mood and cognitive symptoms

differential.name: Normal aging with mild cognitive impairment
differential.why_considered: Many older adults and families worry about dementia when the changes are within the range of normal aging or mild cognitive impairment.

history: Occasional word-finding pauses and misplacing items but able to retrace steps
No interference with work, finances, driving or medications
Family does not report functional decline
Complaints stable over years rather than clearly progressive
exam: Cognitive testing shows mild deficits or is normal for age and education
Independent in all instrumental activities of daily living
No disorientation to date, place or person

differential.name: Medication-induced cognitive impairment
differential.why_considered: Sedatives, anticholinergics and opioids commonly cause or worsen confusion in older adults.
differential.trigger: New or increased sedating or anticholinergic medication before the cognitive change

history: Recent addition or dose increase of a benzodiazepine, opioid, antihistamine, anticholinergic or antipsychotic
Symptoms began within days to weeks of the change
Multiple psychoactive medications (polypharmacy)
Improvement after stopping the offending drug
exam: Sedation, slowed speech or gait instability
Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention or constipation from anticholinergics
Attention and alertness fluctuate with dosing
labs: Medication review is the key test; drug levels when available

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of cognitive slowing, fatigue and depressed mood in older adults.
differential.trigger: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain with cognitive slowing

history: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin
Weight gain despite unchanged diet
Hoarse voice and slowed thinking
Prior thyroid disease, neck radiation or amiodarone use
exam: Bradycardia, delayed relaxation phase of reflexes
Dry coarse skin, thinning hair, periorbital puffiness
Goiter or thyroidectomy scar
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
Anemia and hyperlipidemia may accompany it

differential.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.why_considered: B12 deficiency causes reversible cognitive decline and can occur with a normal CBC.
differential.trigger: Cognitive decline with paresthesias, imbalance or macrocytic anemia

history: Vegan or strict vegetarian diet, or prior gastric or ileal surgery
Metformin or long-term proton pump inhibitor use
Numbness and tingling in the feet, unsteady gait
Sore tongue or glossitis
exam: Decreased vibration and position sense in the feet
Positive Romberg sign, ataxia
Hyperreflexia or extensor plantar response
Pallor or glossitis
labs: Low serum B12; elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are more sensitive

differential.name: Chronic subdural hematoma
differential.why_considered: A treatable structural cause of progressive confusion, especially in older adults and those on anticoagulants.
differential.trigger: Progressive confusion with headache, gait change or a fall weeks earlier

history: Fall or head injury weeks to months earlier, sometimes unwitnessed
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use
Headache, drowsiness or fluctuating alertness
Stepwise rather than smooth decline
exam: Focal weakness, pronator drift or asymmetric reflexes
Papilledema or decreased level of consciousness
Gait apraxia or unsteadiness
imaging: Crescent-shaped extra-axial collection on head CT
Midline shift or effacement of sulci

differential.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
differential.why_considered: A potentially reversible triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline in older adults.
differential.trigger: Magnetic gait with urinary incontinence and cognitive slowing

history: Gait difficulty is the earliest and most prominent symptom
Urinary urgency and incontinence
Cognitive slowing with relatively preserved memory early
Symptoms may fluctuate
exam: Wide-based, shuffling, 'magnetic' gait with difficulty turning
Impaired postural reflexes
Frontal release signs
imaging: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy
Periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensity from transependymal flow

differential.name: Vascular cognitive impairment
differential.why_considered: Cerebrovascular disease is a common contributor to cognitive decline, often mixed with Alzheimer pathology.

history: Stepwise decline with plateaus, often after strokes
Vascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation
Focal neurologic symptoms or transient ischemic attacks
Early gait disturbance and urinary symptoms
exam: Focal deficits such as weakness, sensory loss or visual field cut
Carotid bruits
Pseudobulbar affect or dysarthria
imaging: Multiple lacunar infarcts, cortical infarcts or extensive white matter hyperintensities

differential.name: Lewy body dementia
differential.why_considered: A common neurodegenerative dementia with features that change management and medication safety.

history: Visual hallucinations, often detailed and recurrent
Fluctuating cognition and alertness
REM sleep behavior disorder with dream enactment
Parkinsonism with falls early in the course
Severe sensitivity to antipsychotic medications
exam: Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia
Postural instability with falls
Fluctuating attention during the visit
imaging: Preserved medial temporal volume on MRI

differential.name: Frontotemporal dementia
differential.why_considered: A cause of early-onset dementia with prominent behavioral or language changes rather than memory loss.

history: Onset often before age 65
Personality change, disinhibition, apathy or loss of empathy
Compulsive or repetitive behaviors, dietary changes
Progressive language difficulty with preserved memory early
Family history of early-onset dementia or motor neuron disease
exam: Impaired executive function and social conduct
Preserved orientation and memory early
Motor neuron disease signs in some patients
imaging: Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy on MRI
Frontal or anterior temporal hypometabolism on FDG-PET

differential.name: Neurosyphilis
differential.why_considered: A treatable infection that can present with cognitive decline, personality change and psychiatric symptoms.
differential.trigger: Cognitive decline with risk factors for syphilis, Argyll Robertson pupils or a rash history

history: History of syphilis or genital ulcer, or multiple sexual partners
Psychiatric symptoms, personality change or memory loss
Tremor, unsteady gait or lightning pains
exam: Argyll Robertson pupils (small, irregular, accommodate but do not react)
Tremor, dysarthria, ataxia or hyperreflexia
Optic atrophy or cranial nerve deficits
labs: Positive serum treponemal and nontreponemal tests
Reactive CSF VDRL with lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein

differential.name: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder
differential.why_considered: HIV can cause cognitive decline directly or through opportunistic central nervous system infection.
differential.trigger: Cognitive decline with HIV risk factors, weight loss or systemic symptoms

history: Known HIV infection or risk factors
Weight loss, night sweats, recurrent infections
Progressive cognitive slowing and apathy
exam: Impaired attention and processing speed
Tremor, hyperreflexia or ataxia
Oral thrush or lymphadenopathy
labs: Positive HIV antibody or antigen test
Low CD4 count and elevated viral load
imaging: Diffuse white matter hyperintensities on MRI
Cerebral atrophy out of proportion to age

differential.name: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
differential.why_considered: A rapidly progressive dementia that must be recognized because of its speed and prognosis.
differential.trigger: Dementia progressing over weeks to months with myoclonus and ataxia

history: Rapid progression over weeks to months
Myoclonic jerks, especially startle-induced
Unsteady gait and coordination problems
Behavioral change and insomnia early
exam: Myoclonus, ataxia, extrapyramidal signs
Cognitive decline with preserved awareness until late
Visual disturbances or akinetic mutism late
labs: EEG showing periodic sharp wave complexes
imaging: Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted MRI

severity.mild: Cognitive decline is detectable on testing and interferes with instrumental activities such as finances, medications and driving, but the patient remains independent in basic self-care and can hold a conversation.
severity.moderate: Memory and orientation are clearly impaired; the patient needs help with medications, appointments and some activities of daily living such as dressing or bathing; behavioral symptoms such as apathy, irritability or wandering may appear.
severity.severe: The patient is disoriented to person, place and time, is dependent for most activities of daily living, may be incontinent, and has limited or incoherent speech; behavioral and motor complications are common.
severity.critical: End-stage disease with immobility, dysphagia, recurrent aspiration and infections; death usually results from aspiration pneumonia, sepsis or another intercurrent illness rather than from the dementia itself.

red_flags.finding: Acute onset over hours to days with fluctuating attention
red_flags.meaning: Delirium superimposed on dementia or a non-dementia cause; look for infection, medication, metabolic derangement or withdrawal

red_flags.finding: New focal weakness, sensory loss, aphasia or visual field cut
red_flags.meaning: Stroke or structural lesion; obtain urgent imaging

red_flags.finding: New severe headache, neck stiffness or fever
red_flags.meaning: Central nervous system infection or hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Rapid progression over weeks to months with myoclonus or ataxia
red_flags.meaning: Consider Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, autoimmune encephalitis or central nervous system infection

red_flags.finding: Recent fall or head injury, especially on an anticoagulant
red_flags.meaning: Chronic subdural hematoma; obtain head CT

red_flags.finding: Weight loss, night sweats or focal neurologic signs in a younger patient
red_flags.meaning: Consider HIV, malignancy or opportunistic infection

red_flags.finding: New urinary incontinence with gait deterioration
red_flags.meaning: Consider normal pressure hydrocephalus, which may be reversible
Psychiatric emergency requiring immediate safety planning

complications.name: Delirium superimposed on dementia
clues: New infection, medication or metabolic change

complications.name: Medication adverse effects
clues: Bradycardia or syncope with cholinesterase inhibitors
Worsening confusion after a medication change

complications.name: Caregiver burnout
clues: Caregiver reports exhaustion, depression or resentment

special_populations.differences: The largest group affected; presentation may be dominated by falls, weight loss, incontinence or delirium rather than memory complaints, and polypharmacy and sensory impairment worsen function.
Dementia is very rare in children and usually reflects a metabolic, genetic or neurodegenerative disorder with developmental regression, seizures or loss of previously acquired skills.
Dementia is uncommon in pregnancy; cognitive complaints are more often related to thyroid disease, anemia, mood disorders or eclampsia-related neurologic complications.

Cognitive decline may be due to opportunistic central nervous system infection or HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder and can progress faster; maintain a lower threshold for imaging and CSF studies.
Uremic encephalopathy and dialysis-related fluctuations can mimic dementia; symptoms may wax and wane with dialysis and improve with treatment.
Hepatic encephalopathy causes fluctuating attention and asterixis that can look like dementia but reverses with treatment of the liver disease.
Recurrent hypoglycemia and severe hyperglycemia can cause cognitive symptoms that fluctuate with glucose levels and improve with better control.
Midlife obesity is a modifiable vascular risk factor and is associated with a higher risk of later cognitive decline.

key_questions.question: What changes have you or your family noticed, and when did they start?
key_questions.looking_for: Insidious onset over months to years of memory and thinking problems, not an abrupt change over hours to days

key_questions.question: Is this getting steadily worse over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Slowly progressive decline; stepwise decline suggests vascular disease, rapid decline over weeks suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or another rapidly progressive cause

key_questions.question: Are these problems interfering with your day-to-day life, like managing money, medications or driving?
key_questions.looking_for: Loss of independence in instrumental activities of daily living, which separates dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment

key_questions.question: Do you repeat the same question or story within minutes? Do you misplace items in odd places?
key_questions.looking_for: Short-term memory loss with repetition and misplacing items, typical of Alzheimer disease

key_questions.question: Have you gotten lost in places you know well, like your own neighborhood?
key_questions.looking_for: Getting lost in familiar places, which supports functional impairment and visuospatial involvement

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble finding the right words or naming familiar objects?
key_questions.looking_for: Word-finding difficulty and circumlocution; prominent early language change suggests a frontotemporal disorder

key_questions.question: Have you seen or heard things that others do not see or hear?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, which point to Lewy body dementia

key_questions.question: Do you act out your dreams, such as kicking or shouting while asleep?
key_questions.looking_for: REM sleep behavior disorder, which supports Lewy body dementia and often precedes it

key_questions.question: Has your personality or behavior changed, such as losing interest in things or saying inappropriate things?
key_questions.looking_for: Apathy, disinhibition or loss of empathy, which suggests frontotemporal dementia

key_questions.question: How is your mood? Have you felt down, hopeless or lost interest in things you enjoy?
key_questions.looking_for: Depression, which can mimic dementia and is treatable; also a common comorbidity

key_questions.question: Have you had any sudden confusion, or times when you were less alert and then improved?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluctuating attention and acute onset, which point to delirium rather than dementia

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent fall or hit your head, especially if you take a blood thinner?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic subdural hematoma, a treatable structural cause of progressive confusion

key_questions.question: Have you had any new weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or vision loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal neurologic deficits suggesting stroke, mass lesion or another structural cause

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, night sweats or weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Infection such as HIV or another systemic illness causing cognitive decline

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble with your balance or walking, or any new urinary accidents?
key_questions.looking_for: Gait disturbance with urinary incontinence, which suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus, a potentially reversible cause

key_questions.question: What medical conditions do you have, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation or prior stroke?
key_questions.looking_for: Vascular risk factors that raise the likelihood of vascular contributions to cognitive impairment

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a stroke, transient ischemic attack or head injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior cerebrovascular events or traumatic brain injury, which increase dementia risk

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including over-the-counter sleep aids, allergy medicines and pain medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Sedating or anticholinergic drugs such as diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, benzodiazepines or opioids that can impair cognition

key_questions.question: Have you started any new medication or had a dose change recently?
key_questions.looking_for: A temporal link between a new drug and cognitive change, suggesting medication-induced impairment

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have dementia, especially a parent or sibling, or did anyone develop it before age 65?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of dementia, which raises risk and may suggest a familial or early-onset form

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and have you ever had withdrawal symptoms?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy alcohol use or withdrawal, which can cause cognitive impairment and mimic dementia

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and have you had exposure to solvents or pesticides at work?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable vascular risk factors and occupational exposures associated with cognitive decline

key_questions.question: Who do you live with, and who helps you with things like bills, medications and appointments?
key_questions.looking_for: Level of support at home and safety concerns such as living alone or driving with getting lost

key_questions.question: Do you still drive, and have you had any near-misses or gotten lost while driving?
key_questions.looking_for: Driving safety risk, which affects independence and public safety

key_questions.question: Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or others?
key_questions.looking_for: Suicidal ideation or severe agitation, which is a psychiatric emergency

reasoning_points: Insidious onset over months to years with slowly progressive decline, rather than the acute fluctuating course of delirium
Cognitive impairment in at least one domain (memory, language, executive function, visuospatial ability or attention) documented by history and objective testing
The decline interferes with independence in everyday activities such as finances, medications, driving or appointments
The impairment is not explained by delirium or a major psychiatric disorder such as depression
Reversible causes have been excluded: hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, uremia, glucose abnormalities and medication effects
Structural imaging has excluded treatable lesions such as chronic subdural hematoma, tumor, normal pressure hydrocephalus and stroke
The pattern of deficits and any associated features (visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, stepwise decline, prominent behavioral change) help identify the subtype
Red flags such as rapid progression over weeks, focal neurologic deficits, fever, head trauma or new incontinence with gait change have been considered and addressed

easy: Older adult with insidious, progressive short-term memory loss over years
Family reports repeating questions and getting lost in familiar places
Clear interference with finances and medications
Cognitive testing shows impaired recall that does not improve with cueing
Reversible causes excluded and MRI shows typical atrophy
medium: Older adult with apathy and withdrawal, raising the question of depression versus dementia
Patient with vascular risk factors and a stepwise decline after a stroke
Patient with visual hallucinations, fluctuating alertness and dream enactment suggesting Lewy body dementia
Patient on multiple sedating or anticholinergic medications with cognitive slowing
Cognitive complaints with a normal neurologic exam and only subtle deficits on testing
hard: Very old patient presenting with falls, weight loss or incontinence rather than memory complaints
Delirium superimposed on dementia, with acute worsening and fluctuating attention
Rapidly progressive dementia over weeks with myoclonus and ataxia suggesting Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Early-onset dementia before age 65 with prominent behavioral or language changes suggesting frontotemporal dementia
Gait-predominant presentation with urinary incontinence suggesting normal pressure hydrocephalus
Patient with HIV or another immunocompromising condition and cognitive decline
Cognitive decline in a patient with renal or hepatic impairment where encephalopathy can mimic dementia
